Ephesians — Book introduction (Modern English candidate)

Paul wrote this letter while a prisoner in Rome.

Its purpose appears to have been to strengthen the Ephesians in their faith in Christ.

He wanted them to recognize the greatness of God's love and the dignity and excellence of Jesus Christ, so they would not be shaken by the apparent disgrace of his cross.

Paul taught that they had been saved by grace.

Although they had once lived in a wretched condition, they now enjoyed the same privileges as Jewish believers.

He encouraged them to persevere in their Christian calling and live in a way that agreed with their profession.

That involved faithfully performing both the common duties of Christian living and the particular duties arising from family and social relationships.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA salutation, and an account of saving blessings, as prepared in God's eternal election, as purchased by Christ's blood.1–8And as conveyed in effectual calling: this is applied to the believing Jews, and to the believing Gentiles.9–14The apostle thanks God for their faith and love, and prays for the continuance of their knowledge and hope, with respect to the heavenly inheritance, and to God's powerful working in them.15–23
Grace, peace and a faithful profession (verses 1 and 2)

Every Christian ought to be a saint, someone set apart for God.

Those who do not truly belong to him here will not become saints in heavenly glory.

Genuine saints are faithful believers in Jesus Christ who live consistently with their profession of belonging to him.

Grace means God's undeserved love and favor together with the spiritual blessings that flow from it.

Peace includes the inward and outward blessings that are genuinely good for us.

Grace comes first; peace follows. There is no true peace without grace.

Neither grace nor peace comes from any source apart from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Even the most mature believers need fresh supplies of the Holy Spirit's grace and should long for further growth.

Chosen in Christ for adoption and holiness (verses 3–8)

Spiritual and heavenly blessings are the greatest blessings of all.

Possessing them, we cannot finally be miserable; lacking them, we cannot finally be happy.

These gifts flow from God's gracious decision in Christ before the foundation of the world.

He chose believers to become holy, separated from sin, dedicated to God and sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

Everyone chosen for happiness as the final goal is also chosen for holiness as the appointed path.

In love, God predestined believers to be adopted as his children through faith in Jesus Christ, publicly receiving the privileges of that relationship.

The reconciled, adopted, forgiven sinner therefore gives all the praise to the gracious Father.

His love planned redemption, did not spare his own Son, and brought believers to hear, trust and embrace his salvation.

What rich grace to provide his own Son as our Surety and freely hand him over for us!

This salvation does not encourage wrongdoing.

Instead, it reveals how hateful sin is and how seriously it deserves divine judgment.

The believer's conduct as well as speech should proclaim the glory of God's mercy.

The mystery of redemption and the Spirit's seal (verses 9–14)

God made known to believers the mystery of his sovereign purpose and the way he would redeem and save them.

These truths would have remained hidden forever if the Lord had not revealed them through his written word, the preached gospel and the Spirit of truth.

In his own person, Jesus Christ brought together God and humanity, who had been separated by sin, and satisfied the wrong that caused their separation.

By his Spirit he produces faith and love, uniting us to God and to one another.

Christ distributes his blessings according to his gracious will.

Through his divine teaching, some are brought to see the glory of truths that others continue to reject or even mock.

What a gracious promise that the Holy Spirit will be given to those who ask for him!

The Spirit's sanctifying and comforting work seals believers as God's children and heirs of heaven.

His present blessings are the first fruits of everlasting happiness.

We were created and redeemed for this purpose.

Everything God has done for us aims ultimately at the praise of his glory.

Paul prays for greater understanding and hope (verses 15–23)

God has stored up every spiritual blessing for us in his Son, Jesus Christ.

He calls us to seek and receive those blessings through prayer.

Even the strongest Christians still need others to pray for them.

When we hear encouraging news about Christian friends, we should respond by praying for their continued growth.

Genuine believers still need much heavenly wisdom.

Even the best of us resist God's rule at times, though submitting to him is the only path to true rest.

How often do we trade our inward peace for a brief pleasure!

If we spent less time arguing and more time praying with and for one another, we would see more clearly the hope of our calling and the riches of God's glorious inheritance.

We should long to experience the mighty power of divine grace beginning and continuing the work of faith within us.

It is extraordinarily difficult for a soul to trust Christ completely and place every hope of everlasting life upon his righteousness alone.

Nothing less than God's almighty power can produce such faith.

Christ supplies the needs of those who trust him and gives his blessings abundantly.

Being united to Christ himself, we share the fullness of grace and glory found in him.

How foolish to seek righteousness apart from him!

If we understood what we have been called to receive, we would eagerly seek Christ.

As we recognize our weakness and the strength of our spiritual enemies, we see more clearly the greatness of the power that converts the believer and guarantees the completion of salvation.

This knowledge should move us, through love, to live for our Redeemer's glory.
classic_reading:
[Eph.1.1-Eph.1.2]
Ephesians
This epistle was written when St. Paul was a prisoner at Rome. The design appears to be to strengthen the Ephesians in the faith of Christ, and to give exalted views of the love of God, and of the dignity and excellence of Christ, fortifying their minds against the scandal of the cross. He shows that they were saved by grace, and that however wretched they once were, they now had equal privileges with the Jews. He encourages them to persevere in their Christian calling, and urges them to walk in a manner becoming their profession, faithfully discharging the general and common duties of religion, and the special duties of particular relations.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
A salutation, and an account of saving blessings, as prepared in God's eternal election, as purchased by Christ's blood. | (1-8) |
And as conveyed in effectual calling: this is applied to the believing Jews, and to the believing Gentiles. | (9-14) |
The apostle thanks God for their faith and love, and prays for the continuance of their knowledge and hope, with respect to the heavenly inheritance, and to God's powerful working in them. | (15-23) |
Verses 1-2
All Christians must be saints; if they come not under that character on earth, they will never be saints in glory. Those are not saints, who are not faithful, believing in Christ, and true to the profession they make of relation to their Lord. By grace, understand the free and undeserved love and favour of God, and those graces of the Spirit which come from it; by peace, all other blessings, spiritual and temporal, the fruits of the former. No peace without grace. No peace, nor grace, but from God the Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ; and the best saints need fresh supplies of the graces of the Spirit, and desire to grow.
[Eph.1.3-Eph.1.8]
Verses 3-8
Spiritual and heavenly blessings are the best blessings; with which we cannot be miserable, and without which we cannot but be so. This was from the choice of them in Christ, before the foundation of the world, that they should be made holy by separation from sin, being set apart to God, and sanctified by the Holy Spirit, in consequence of their election in Christ. All who are chosen to happiness as the end, are chosen to holiness as the means. In love they were predestinated, or fore-ordained, to be adopted as children of God by faith in Christ Jesus, and to be openly admitted to the privileges of that high relation to himself. The reconciled and adopted believer, the pardoned sinner, gives all the praise of his salvation to his gracious Father. His love appointed this method of redemption, spared not his own Son, and brought believers to hear and embrace this salvation. It was rich grace to provide such a surety as his own Son, and freely to deliver him up. This method of grace gives no encouragement to evil, but shows sin in all its hatefulness, and how it deserves vengeance. The believer's actions, as well as his words, declare the praises of Divine mercy.
[Eph.1.9-Eph.1.14]
Verses 9-14
Blessings were made known to believers, by the Lord's showing to them the mystery of his sovereign will, and the method of redemption and salvation. But these must have been for ever hidden from us, if God had not made them known by his written word, preached gospel, and Spirit of truth. Christ united the two differing parties, God and man, in his own person, and satisfied for that wrong which caused the separation. He wrought, by his Spirit, those graces of faith and love, whereby we are made one with God, and among ourselves. He dispenses all his blessings, according to his good pleasure. His Divine teaching led whom he pleased to see the glory of those truths, which others were left to blaspheme. What a gracious promise that is, which secures the gift of the Holy Ghost to those who ask him! The sanctifying and comforting influences of the Holy Spirit seal believers as the children of God, and heirs of heaven. These are the first-fruits of holy happiness. For this we were made, and for this we were redeemed; this is the great design of God in all that he has done for us; let all be ascribed unto the praise of his glory.
[Eph.1.15-Eph.1.23]
Verses 15-23
God has laid up spiritual blessings for us in his Son the Lord Jesus; but requires us to draw them out and fetch them in by prayer. Even the best Christians need to be prayed for: and while we hear of the welfare of Christian friends, we should pray for them. Even true believers greatly want heavenly wisdom. Are not the best of us unwilling to come under God's yoke, though there is no other way to find rest for the soul? Do we not for a little pleasure often part with our peace? And if we dispute less, and prayed more with and for each other, we should daily see more and more what is the hope of our calling, and the riches of the Divine glory in this inheritance. It is desirable to feel the mighty power of Divine grace, beginning and carrying on the work of faith in our souls. But it is difficult to bring a soul to believe fully in Christ, and to venture its all, and the hope of eternal life, upon his righteousness. Nothing less than Almighty power will work this in us. Here is signified that it is Christ the Saviour, who supplies all the necessities of those who trust in him, and gives them all blessings in the richest abundance. And by being partakers of Christ himself, we come to be filled with the fulness of grace and glory in him. How then do those forget themselves who seek for righteousness out of him! This teaches us to come to Christ. And did we know what we are called to, and what we might find in him, surely we should come and be suitors to him. When feeling our weakness and the power of our enemies, we most perceive the greatness of that mighty power which effects the conversion of the believer, and is engaged to perfect his salvation. Surely this will constrain us by love to live to our Redeemer's glory.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe riches of God's grace towards men, shown from their deplorable state by nature, and the happy change Divine grace makes in them.1–10The Ephesians called to reflect on their state of heathenism.11–13And the privileges and blessings of the gospel.14–22
Saved by grace from spiritual death (verses 1–10)

Sin is death to the soul.

Someone dead in trespasses and sins has no appetite for genuine spiritual happiness.

Seeing a dead body fills us with dread. The undying human spirit has departed, leaving behind the ruined remains of its earthly life.

But if we understood the matter correctly, we would be far more deeply disturbed by a soul spiritually dead in sin.

Living in sin means adopting the patterns of this world.

Wicked people become slaves of Satan, who works through proud and sinful desires and rules in hearts that resist God.

Scripture teaches that people are naturally children of disobedience and exposed to wrath, whether their sins take the form of bodily indulgence or the equally serious pride of the spirit.

What reason we all have to seek the grace that can turn children of wrath into God's children and heirs of glory!

The source of God's mercies is his great love and rich compassion.

Every genuinely converted sinner is a sinner saved from both sin and wrath.

Saving grace is God's free, undeserved favor.

He saves us not by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.

Grace also gives the soul new life.

A regenerated person now lives in holiness, having been born of God.

Through God's pardoning and justifying grace, that person is freed from sin's guilt.

While sinners roll in the dust, believers sanctified by Christ's grace are raised spiritually to sit in heavenly places, no longer ruled by this world's values.

God's past acts of conversion and salvation encourage future generations to hope in his mercy and grace.

Our faith, conversion and eternal salvation are not works we have accomplished.

No one can boast.

Everything is the gift of God, accomplished as he gives life through his power.

God also prepared us for good works.

He gives us knowledge of his will, while the Holy Spirit transforms us so that we increasingly glorify him through holy conduct and perseverance.

This teaching cannot honestly be used to justify wrongdoing.

Anyone claiming that salvation by grace encourages sin has misunderstood or rejected Scripture's teaching.

Remember what it meant to be far from Christ (verses 11–13)

Christ and his covenant are the foundation of all Christian hope.

Paul described the Gentiles' former condition in terrible terms.

But who could rescue themselves from that condition?

How sad that the same description may apply even to some people who have been baptized in Christ's name while still lacking genuine faith.

Consider the horror of being permanently separated from God's people, cut off from the body of Christ, excluded from the covenant of promise and left with no hope and no Savior.

A person in that condition has no fellowship with God as a loving Father and must face his righteous judgment.

What genuine believer can think about that danger without trembling?

Salvation is far from those who persist in wickedness.

Yet God comes close to help his own people through Christ's suffering and death.

Christ makes peace and opens access to the Father (verses 14–18)

Jesus Christ made peace through the sacrifice of himself.

In every sense Christ himself is our peace.

He is the author, center and substance of our reconciliation with God.

He also unites believing Gentiles and Jews into one church.

Through Christ's person, sacrifice and mediation, sinners are allowed to approach God as Father and are welcomed into his presence.

Their worship and service are received under the Holy Spirit's instruction, because they are united to the Father and the Son.

Christ purchased the right of access to God.

The Spirit gives us the desire to come, the strength to come and grace to serve acceptably.

One household and one holy temple (verses 19–22)

Paul described the church through several pictures.

It is a city: everyone truly converted receives the rights of citizenship.

It is a family household: believers become members of God's own family—his servants and children.

It is a building founded upon the teaching of Jesus Christ, proclaimed through Old Testament prophets and New Testament apostles.

God now dwells within every believer.

Through the power and presence of the Holy Spirit, God's people become his holy temple.
classic_reading:
[Eph.2.1-Eph.2.10]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
The riches of God's grace towards men, shown from their deplorable state by nature, and the happy change Divine grace makes in them. | (1-10) |
The Ephesians called to reflect on their state of heathenism. | (11-13) |
And the privileges and blessings of the gospel. | (14-22) |
Verses 1-10
Sin is the death of the soul. A man dead in trespasses and sins has no desire for spiritual pleasures. When we look upon a corpse, it gives an awful feeling. A never-dying spirit is now fled, and has left nothing but the ruins of a man. But if we viewed things aright, we should be far more affected by the thought of a dead soul, a lost, fallen spirit. A state of sin is a state of conformity to this world. Wicked men are slaves to Satan. Satan is the author of that proud, carnal disposition which there is in ungodly men; he rules in the hearts of men. From Scripture it is clear, that whether men have been most prone to sensual or to spiritual wickedness, all men, being naturally children of disobedience, are also by nature children of wrath. What reason have sinners, then, to seek earnestly for that grace which will make them, of children of wrath, children of God and heirs of glory! God's eternal love or good-will toward his creatures, is the fountain whence all his mercies flow to us; and that love of God is great love, and that mercy is rich mercy. And every converted sinner is a saved sinner; delivered from sin and wrath. The grace that saves is the free, undeserved goodness and favour of God; and he saves, not by the works of the law, but through faith in Christ Jesus. Grace in the soul is a new life in the soul. A regenerated sinner becomes a living soul; he lives a life of holiness, being born of God: he lives, being delivered from the guilt of sin, by pardoning and justifying grace. Sinners roll themselves in the dust; sanctified souls sit in heavenly places, are raised above this world, by Christ's grace. The goodness of God in converting and saving sinners heretofore, encourages others in after-time, to hope in his grace and mercy. Our faith, our conversion, and our eternal salvation, are not of works, lest any man should boast. These things are not brought to pass by any thing done by us, therefore all boasting is shut out. All is the free gift of God, and the effect of being quickened by his power. It was his purpose, to which he prepared us, by blessing us with the knowledge of his will, and his Holy Spirit producing such a change in us, that we should glorify God by our good conversation, and perseverance in holiness. None can from Scripture abuse this doctrine, or accuse it of any tendency to evil. All who do so, are without excuse.
[Eph.2.11-Eph.2.13]
Verses 11-13
Christ and his covenant are the foundation of all the Christian's hopes. A sad and terrible description is here; but who is able to remove himself out of it? Would that this were not a true description of many baptized in the name of Christ. Who can, without trembling, reflect upon the misery of a person, separated for ever from the people of God, cut off from the body of Christ, fallen from the covenant of promise, having no hope, no Saviour, and without any God but a God of vengeance, to all eternity? To have no part in Christ! What true Christian can hear this without horror? Salvation is far from the wicked; but God is a help at hand to his people; and this is by the sufferings and death of Christ.
[Eph.2.14-Eph.2.18]
Verses 14-18
Jesus Christ made peace by the sacrifice of himself; in every sense Christ was their Peace, the author, centre, and substance of their being at peace with God, and of their union with the Jewish believers in one church. Through the person, sacrifice, and mediation of Christ, sinners are allowed to draw near to God as a Father, and are brought with acceptance into his presence, with their worship and services, under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, as one with the Father and the Son. Christ purchased leave for us to come to God; and the Spirit gives a heart to come, and strength to come, and then grace to serve God acceptably.
[Eph.2.19-Eph.2.22]
Verses 19-22
The church is compared to a city, and every converted sinner is free of it. It is also compared to a house, and every converted sinner is one of the family; a servant, and a child in God's house. The church is also compared to a building, founded on the doctrine of Christ; delivered by the prophets of the Old Testament, and the apostles of the New. God dwells in all believers now; they become the temple of God through the working of the blessed Spirit. Let us then ask if our hopes are fixed on Christ, according to the doctrine of his word? Have we devoted ourselves as holy temples to God through him? Are we habitations of God by the Spirit, are we spiritually-minded, and do we bring forth the fruits of the Spirit? Let us take heed not to grieve the holy Comforter. Let us desire his gracious presence, and his influences upon our hearts. Let us seek to discharge the duties allotted to us, to the glory of God.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe apostle sets forth his office, and his qualifications for it, and his call to it.1–7Also the noble purposes answered by it.8–12He prays for the Ephesians.13–19And adds a thanksgiving.20, 21
Paul's calling to make the gospel mystery known (verses 1–7)

Paul was imprisoned because he had faithfully preached God's truth.

Yet he was a prisoner of Jesus Christ, protected and cared for by the very Lord for whose sake he suffered.

The gospel's promises and joyful announcement all come from God's rich grace.

Through that message, the Holy Spirit ordinarily produces grace in human souls.

The mystery Paul described was God's once-hidden purpose of salvation through Jesus Christ.

Earlier generations had not received such a clear and full account of it as was given to the New Testament apostles and prophets.

A central part of the revelation entrusted to Paul was that Gentiles would be called to salvation through faith in Christ.

The gifts of divine grace are accompanied by God's effective power.

The Lord not only appointed Paul to his apostolic office.

He also equipped him to carry out its responsibilities.

The unsearchable riches of Christ are announced (verses 8–12)

When God gives people an honorable calling, he often makes them humble in their own eyes.

And where he gives the grace of humility, he gives the other graces needed for duty.

Notice how magnificently Paul describes the unsearchable riches of Jesus Christ!

Many have not received these riches.

Yet what a privilege even to hear them proclaimed and freely offered!

Those who refuse such a gift have no reason to blame its Giver.

Both the first creation—when God brought the world into existence from nothing—and the new creation, when sinners are transformed by converting grace, come from God through Jesus Christ.

Christ's spiritual riches remain as vast and certain as ever.

Angels marvel at God's wisdom in redeeming his church.

Yet self-satisfied and worldly people often dismiss that same wisdom as foolishness.

Paul prays for strength and a deeper knowledge of Christ's love (verses 13–19)

Paul seemed more troubled by the possibility that the Ephesians would become discouraged because of his suffering than by the suffering he had to endure himself.

He therefore asked for spiritual blessings, the greatest gifts of all.

He prayed for strength through God's Spirit in the inner person.

This includes strength of soul and faith so that believers can serve God and perform their duties.

When Christ's law is written upon the heart and his love is poured into it, Christ lives there.

Where his Spirit dwells, Christ himself dwells.

We should desire that good affections become deeply rooted and stable within us.

How wonderful to enjoy a settled awareness of God's love for us in Christ!

Consider the dimensions Paul uses to describe that love.

Its breadth reaches people of every nation and social rank.

Its length continues from eternity past to eternity future.

Its depth reaches people sunk in the deepest sin and misery.

Its height raises them into heavenly happiness and glory.

Those who receive grace upon grace from Christ's fullness can be described as being filled with God's fullness.

Should that not satisfy the human heart?

Why do we try to complete our happiness by filling ourselves with a thousand worthless distractions?

End prayer with praise (verses 20 and 21)

Prayer should naturally lead to thanksgiving and praise.

Because of what Christ has already accomplished in our souls, we may ask and expect even more from his grace.

The conversion of sinners and the comfort of believers will bring glory to Christ forever.
classic_reading:
[Eph.3.1-Eph.3.7]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The apostle sets forth his office, and his qualifications for it, and his call to it. | (1-7) |
Also the noble purposes answered by it. | (8-12) |
He prays for the Ephesians. | (13-19) |
And adds a thanksgiving. | (20-21) |
Verses 1-7
For having preached the doctrine of truth, the apostle was a prisoner, but a prisoner of Jesus Christ; the object of special protection and care, while thus suffering for him. All the gracious offers of the gospel, and the joyful tidings it contains, come from the rich grace of God; it is the great means by which the Spirit works grace in the souls of men. The mystery, is that secret, hidden purpose of salvation through Christ. This was not so fully and clearly shown in the ages before Christ, as unto the prophets of the New Testament. This was the great truth made known to the apostle, that God would call the Gentiles to salvation by faith in Christ. An effectual working of Divine power attends the gifts of Divine grace. As God appointed Paul to the office, so he qualified him for it.
[Eph.3.8-Eph.3.12]
Verses 8-12
Those whom God advances to honourable employments, he makes low in their own eyes; and where God gives grace to be humble, there he gives all other needful grace. How highly he speaks of Jesus Christ; the unsearchable riches of Christ! Though many are not enriched with these riches; yet how great a favour to have them preached among us, and to have an offer of them! And if we are not enriched with them it is our own fault. The first creation, when God made all things out of nothing, and the new creation, whereby sinners are made new creatures by converting grace, are of God by Jesus Christ. His riches are as unsearchable and as sure as ever, yet while angels adore the wisdom of God in the redemption of his church, the ignorance of self-wise and carnal men deems the whole to be foolishness.
[Eph.3.13-Eph.3.19]
Verses 13-19
The apostle seems to be more anxious lest the believers should be discouraged and faint upon his tribulations, than for what he himself had to bear. He asks for spiritual blessings, which are the best blessings. Strength from the Spirit of God in the inner man; strength in the soul; the strength of faith, to serve God, and to do our duty. If the law of Christ is written in our hearts, and the love of Christ is shed abroad there, then Christ dwells there. Where his Spirit dwells, there he dwells. We should desire that good affections may be fixed in us. And how desirable to have a fixed sense of the love of God in Christ to our souls! How powerfully the apostle speaks of the love of Christ! The breadth shows its extent to all nations and ranks; the length, that it continues from everlasting to everlasting; the depth, its saving those who are sunk into the depths of sin and misery; the height, its raising them up to heavenly happiness and glory. Those who receive grace for grace from Christ's fulness, may be said to be filled with the fulness of God. Should not this satisfy man? Must he needs fill himself with a thousand trifles, fancying thereby to complete his happiness?
[Eph.3.20-Eph.3.21]
Verses 20-21
It is proper always to end prayers with praises. Let us expect more, and ask for more, encouraged by what Christ has already done for our souls, being assured that the conversion of sinners, and the comfort of believers, will be to his glory, for ever and ever.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesExhortations to mutual forbearance and union.1–6To a due use of spiritual gifts and graces.7–16To purity and holiness.17–24And to take heed of the sins practised among the heathen.25–32
Walk together in humility and unity (verses 1–6)

Few duties are urged more strongly in Scripture than living in a manner worthy of the calling to Christ's kingdom and glory.

Humility opposes pride.

Gentleness makes us reluctant to provoke others and slow to become offended or angry.

We discover so many faults in ourselves—faults we sometimes find hard even to forgive ourselves—that we should not be surprised to find weaknesses in others that are difficult to overlook.

All believers hope in one Christ and look forward to one heaven.

They should therefore be of one heart.

They share one faith in its object, Author, nature and power, receiving the same great truths of religion.

They have been admitted into the church through one baptism with water, in the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, as a sign of regeneration.

God the Father dwells in believers as within his holy temple, through his Spirit and special grace.

Christ gives different gifts for the body's growth (verses 7–16)

Every true believer receives some measure of grace for the mutual good of God's people.

Christ distributes his gifts in the way that seems best to him.

He received gifts and graces to give them to his church, especially the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The knowledge required is more than merely understanding Christian ideas or acknowledging intellectually that Christ is the Son of God.

It produces trust and obedience.

There is fullness in Christ, and every believer receives a measure from that fullness according to God's wise decision.

Yet we will not reach complete maturity until heaven.

God's children continue growing throughout this life, and their growth brings glory to Christ.

The more someone uses their particular responsibilities and gifts for the spiritual benefit of other people, the stronger the evidence that genuine Christian love has taken root in the heart.

Put off the old life and put on the new (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.17-Eph.4.24" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 17–24</reference>)

Speaking by Christ's authority, Paul urged the Ephesians not to live like unbelieving Gentiles who followed empty ideas and sinful desires.

People everywhere still live under the influence of confused, worthless thoughts.

We therefore need to distinguish genuine Christian life from a merely Christian name.

Without saving knowledge, people remain in darkness and often prefer the darkness to the light.

They resist holiness.

Yet holiness is what God commands and approves, and it reflects something of his purity, righteousness, truth and goodness.

The gospel's truth becomes especially beautiful when seen in Jesus himself.

Our sinful nature is described as an old person, made up of many related desires and habits that reinforce one another.

Corrupt desires are deceptive.

They promise happiness but actually deepen misery and lead toward destruction unless they are resisted and put to death.

We must take them off like a dirty, worn-out garment.

But it is not enough to abandon corrupt principles.

We must receive new and gracious principles in their place.

The new person is a renewed nature, created through God's mighty power and governed by regenerating grace.

That grace enables a new life of genuine righteousness and holiness.

Speak truth, control anger and work honestly (verses 25–28)

Paul gave practical examples of conduct that should adorn a Christian profession.

Reject falsehood.

Do not flatter or deceive people.

God's children should hate lying and refuse to practice it.

We must also guard against uncontrolled anger.

Sometimes wrong behavior must be confronted.

Yet even when displeasure is justified, we must express correction without sinning.

We give the devil an opportunity when early sinful impulses no longer grieve us, when we consent to them or when we repeat evil actions.

Resist sin and avoid even circumstances that invite wrongdoing.

Idleness creates temptation, including temptation to steal.

People should work diligently not only to provide for themselves but also to have something with which to help those in need.

What should we think of professing Christians who become rich through fraud, exploitation and deceit?

Charitable gifts cannot be acceptable when obtained through dishonesty or robbery.

God rejects the attempt to make an offering out of stolen goods.

Use words that build up and forgive as God forgave (verses 29–32)

Corrupt speech comes from corruption in the speaker and harms the thoughts and conduct of listeners.

Christians should avoid such talk.

Instead, through their conversations they should encourage people to think seriously and should strengthen, warn and comfort fellow believers.

We are called to be kind to one another.

True kindness grows out of love within the heart and expresses itself through humble, courteous conduct.

Notice how God's forgiveness becomes the reason for our forgiveness.

We had no rightful cause to sin against him, yet he forgave us.

We therefore ought to forgive other people as he has forgiven us.

Lies, corrupt speech and conversation that arouses sinful desires grieve God's Holy Spirit.

So do bitterness, rage, uncontrolled anger, shouting, slander and malice.

Do not provoke the holy and blessed Spirit to withdraw his gracious influences and felt presence.

Our bodies will be redeemed from the grave at the resurrection.

Wherever the Holy Spirit lives as the Sanctifier, his presence is the pledge of the joy and glory of that future redemption.

How lost we would be if God withdrew his Holy Spirit from us!

[Eph.4.1-Eph.4.6]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
Exhortations to mutual forbearance and union. | (1-6) |
To a due use of spiritual gifts and graces. | (7-16) |
To purity and holiness. | (17-24) |
And to take heed of the sins practised among the heathen. | (25-32) |
Verses 1-6
Nothing is pressed more earnestly in the Scriptures, than to walk as becomes those called to Christ's kingdom and glory. By lowliness, understand humility, which is opposed to pride. By meekness, that excellent disposition of soul, which makes men unwilling to provoke, and not easily to be provoked or offended. We find much in ourselves for which we can hardly forgive ourselves; therefore we must not be surprised if we find in others that which we think it hard to forgive. There is one Christ in whom all believers hope, and one heaven they are all hoping for; therefore they should be of one heart. They had all one faith, as to its object, Author, nature, and power. They all believed the same as to the great truths of religion; they had all been admitted into the church by one baptism, with water, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, as the sign of regeneration. In all believers God the Father dwells, as in his holy temple, by his Spirit and special grace.
[Eph.4.7-Eph.4.16]
Verses 7-16
Unto every believer is given some gift of grace, for their mutual help. All is given as seems best to Christ to bestow upon every one. He received for them, that he might give to them, a large measure of gifts and graces; particularly the gift of the Holy Ghost. Not a mere head knowledge, or bare acknowledging Christ to be the Son of God, but such as brings trust and obedience. There is a fulness in Christ, and a measure of that fulness given in the counsel of God to every believer; but we never come to the perfect measure till we come to heaven. God's children are growing, as long as they are in this world; and the Christian's growth tends to the glory of Christ. The more a man finds himself drawn out to improve in his station, and according to his measure, all that he has received, to the spiritual good of others, he may the more certainly believe that he has the grace of sincere love and charity rooted in his heart. ( [Eph.4.17-Eph.4.24] Ep 4:17-24)
[Eph.4.17-Eph.4.24]
Verses 17-24
The apostle charged the Ephesians in the name and by the authority of the Lord Jesus, that having professed the gospel, they should not be as the unconverted Gentiles, who walked in vain fancies and carnal affections. Do not men, on every side, walk in the vanity of their minds? Must not we then urge the distinction between real and nominal Christians? They were void of all saving knowledge; they sat in darkness, and loved it rather than light. They had a dislike and hatred to a life of holiness, which is not only the way of life God requires and approves, and by which we live to him, but which has some likeness to God himself in his purity, righteousness, truth, and goodness. The truth of Christ appears in its beauty and power, when it appears as in Jesus. The corrupt nature is called a man; like the human body, it is of divers parts, supporting and strengthening one another. Sinful desires are deceitful lusts; they promise men happiness, but render them more miserable; and bring them to destruction, if not subdued and mortified. These therefore must be put off, as an old garment, a filthy garment; they must be subdued and mortified. But it is not enough to shake off corrupt principles; we must have gracious ones. By the new man, is meant the new nature, the new creature, directed by a new principle, even regenerating grace, enabling a man to lead a new life of righteousness and holiness. This is created, or brought forth by God's almighty power.
[Eph.4.25-Eph.4.28]
Verses 25-28
Notice the particulars wherewith we should adorn our Christian profession. Take heed of every thing contrary to truth. No longer flatter or deceive others. God's people are children who will not lie, who dare not lie, who hate and abhor lying. Take heed of anger and ungoverned passions. If there is just occasion to express displeasure at what is wrong, and to reprove, see that it be without sin. We give place to the devil, when the first motions of sin are not grievous to our souls; when we consent to them; and when we repeat an evil deed. This teaches that as sin, if yielded unto, lets in the devil upon us, we are to resist it, keeping from all appearance of evil. Idleness makes thieves. Those who will not work, expose themselves to temptations to steal. Men ought to be industrious, that they may do some good, and that they may be kept from temptation. They must labour, not only that they may live honestly, but that they may have to give to the wants of others. What then must we think of those called Christians, who grow rich by fraud, oppression, and deceitful practices! Alms, to be accepted of God, must not be gained by unrighteousness and robbery, but by honesty and industry. God hates robbery for burnt-offerings.
[Eph.4.29-Eph.4.32]
Verses 29-32
Filthy words proceed from corruption in the speaker, and they corrupt the minds and manners of those who hear them: Christians should beware of all such discourse. It is the duty of Christians to seek, by the blessing of God, to bring persons to think seriously, and to encourage and warn believers by their conversation. Be ye kind one to another. This sets forth the principle of love in the heart, and the outward expression of it, in a humble, courteous behaviour. Mark how God's forgiveness causes us to forgive. God forgives us, though we had no cause to sin against him. We must forgive, as he has forgiven us. All lying, and corrupt communications, that stir up evil desires and lusts, grieve the Spirit of God. Corrupt passions of bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, evil-speaking, and malice, grieve the Holy Spirit. Provoke not the holy, blessed Spirit of God to withdraw his presence and his gracious influences. The body will be redeemed from the power of the grave at the resurrection day. Wherever that blessed Spirit dwells as a Sanctifier, he is the earnest of all the joys and glories of that redemption day; and we should be undone, should God take away his Holy Spirit from us.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesExhortation to brotherly love.1, 2Cautions against several sins.3–14Directions to a contrary behaviour, and to relative duties.15–21The duties of wives and husbands are enforced by the spiritual relation between Christ and the church.22–33
Imitate God's forgiving love (verses 1 and 2)

God has forgiven believers for Christ's sake.

Therefore we should imitate God, especially in his love and willingness to forgive.

This is how beloved children should resemble their heavenly Father.

God's love shines most clearly in the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

We should continually consider the greatness of that love and shape our conduct by it.

Live as children of light (verses 3–14)

Sinful sexual desires must be opposed and put away.

We should fear and detest the sins Paul lists.

The warnings address not only obvious acts of wrongdoing but also practices many people consider unimportant.

Corrupt speech is not useful.

It pollutes those who speak and harms those who listen.

Christian joy ought to be expressed through words that contribute to God's glory.

A greedy person makes money into an idol, transferring to wealth the hope, confidence and happiness that belong to God alone.

Those who surrender themselves to sinful desires or love of the world do not belong to the kingdom of grace and will not enter the kingdom of glory.

Yet even people guilty of dreadful sins can become children of obedience when they repent and believe the gospel.

God's wrath is then turned from them.

How dare we treat lightly the very sins that call down his just judgment?

Sinners resemble people walking in darkness.

They do not understand where they are going or the consequences of their actions.

But God brings about a wonderful change through grace.

Believers must walk as children of light, with knowledge and holiness.

Works of darkness are unfruitful, whatever profit they seem to offer, because they end in ruin for those who refuse repentance.

We may share in other people's sins in many ways: through praise, advice, agreement or hiding their wrongdoing.

If we participate in their sins, we should fear sharing in their judgment.

Henry also says we should rebuke wrongdoing rather than quietly approve it.

A good person may be ashamed even to speak about sins that others shamelessly commit.

It is not enough merely to recognize that a behavior seems shameful.

We must understand that it violates God's holy law.

Like the prophets and apostles, we should call those asleep and dead in sin to wake up and rise, so that Christ may give them light.

Use your time well and seek the Spirit's fullness (verses 15–21)

Another safeguard against sin is careful, thoughtful living.

Without watchfulness, a person cannot preserve purity of heart and conduct.

Time is a gift entrusted to us by God.

When used outside his purposes, it is wasted.

If we have wasted much of our past, we should become more diligent in the time that remains.

Many dying people would gladly give the whole world to recover a little time.

Yet how little we value it now, and how freely we spend it on worthless things!

People often complain about the wickedness of the age.

It would be better if their concern moved them to redeem the time.

Neglecting our souls and remaining ignorant of duty reveal profound foolishness.

Drunkenness rarely comes alone.

It leads people into further sins and provokes God's displeasure.

The person ruled by drink becomes a terrible example to family and community and rushes toward ruin.

When exhausted or sad, we should not try to lift our spirits through intoxicating drink, which can deepen the misery.

Instead, seek through earnest prayer to be filled with the Holy Spirit, and avoid grieving our gracious Comforter.

All God's people have reason to sing with joy.

Even when we are not singing aloud, we should remain continually thankful.

There is never a shortage of reasons for gratitude—even during hardship—because God's dealings have a gracious purpose for his people.

He guides believers away from sin and teaches them to submit to one another in the duties he has commanded, for his glory and their mutual good.

Marriage reflects Christ's union with the church (verses 22–33)

Henry explains the wife's duty as submitting to her husband in the Lord, honoring and obeying him from a principle of love.

He describes the husband's duty as loving his wife.

The example for that love is Christ's love for the church: genuine, pure and constant despite her shortcomings.

Christ gave himself for the church so that he might sanctify her in this life and glorify her in the world to come.

He grants believers a principle of holiness and delivers them from sin's guilt, pollution and rule through the work of the Holy Spirit.

Baptismal water is the outward sign of that inward work.

The church and its members will not be entirely without fault until the day of heavenly glory.

But only those being sanctified now will be glorified then.

Paul's reference to Adam's words has a literal meaning about marriage.

It also has an additional spiritual meaning, as marriage provides a picture of the union between Christ and his church.

Human husbands and wives will both have weaknesses and failures in the present life.

Those imperfections do not cancel their married relationship.

All the responsibilities of marriage can be summarized by unity and love.

As we worship and rejoice in Christ's gracious, self-giving love, let husbands and wives learn their corresponding duties toward one another.

Such faithfulness can prevent many evils and spare families a great deal of pain.
classic_reading:
[Eph.5.1-Eph.5.2]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Exhortation to brotherly love.
(1-2)
Cautions against several sins.
(3-14)
Directions to a contrary behaviour, and to relative duties.
(15-21)
The duties of wives and husbands are enforced by the spiritual relation between Christ and the church.
(22-33)
Verses 1-2
Because God, for Christ's sake, has forgiven you, therefore be ye followers of God, imitators of God. Resemble him especially in his love and pardoning goodness, as becomes those beloved by their heavenly Father. In Christ's sacrifice his love triumphs, and we are to consider it fully.
[Eph.5.3-Eph.5.14]
Verses 3-14
Filthy lusts must be rooted out. These sins must be dreaded and detested. Here are not only cautions against gross acts of sin, but against what some may make light of. But these things are so far from being profitable. that they pollute and poison the hearers. Our cheerfulness should show itself as becomes Christians, in what may tend to God's glory. A covetous man makes a god of his money; places that hope, confidence, and delight, in worldly good, which should be in God only. Those who allow themselves, either in the lusts of the flesh or the love of the world, belong not to the kingdom of grace, nor shall they come to the kingdom of glory. When the vilest transgressors repent and believe the gospel, they become children of obedience, from whom God's wrath is turned away. Dare we make light of that which brings down the wrath of God? Sinners, like men in the dark, are going they know not whither, and doing they know not what. But the grace of God wrought a mighty change in the souls of many. Walk as children of light, as having knowledge and holiness. These works of darkness are unfruitful, whatever profit they may boast; for they end in the destruction of the impenitent sinner. There are many ways of abetting, or taking part in the sins of others; by commendation, counsel, consent, or concealment. And if we share with others in their sins, we must expect to share in their plagues. If we do not reprove the sins of others, we have fellowship with them. A good man will be ashamed to speak of what many wicked men are not ashamed to do. We must have not only a sight and a knowledge that sin is sin, and in some measure shameful, but see it as a breach of God's holy law. After the example of prophets and apostles, we should call on those asleep and dead in sin, to awake and arise, that Christ may give them light.
[Eph.5.15-Eph.5.21]
Verses 15-21
Another remedy against sin, is care, or caution, it being impossible else to maintain purity of heart and life. Time is a talent given us by God, and it is misspent and lost when not employed according to his design. If we have lost our time heretofore, we must double our diligence for the future. Of that time which thousands on a dying bed would gladly redeem at the price of the whole world, how little do men think, and to what trifles they daily sacrifice it! People are very apt to complain of bad times; it were well if that stirred them more to redeem time. Be not unwise. Ignorance of our duty, and neglect of our souls, show the greatest folly. Drunkenness is a sin that never goes alone, but carries men into other evils; it is a sin very provoking to God. The drunkard holds out to his family and to the world the sad spectacle of a sinner hardened beyond what is common, and hastening to perdition. When afflicted or weary, let us not seek to raise our spirits by strong drink, which is hateful and hurtful, and only ends in making sorrows more felt. But by fervent prayer let us seek to be filled with the Spirit, and to avoid whatever may grieve our gracious Comforter. All God's people have reason to sing for joy. Though we are not always singing, we should be always giving thanks; we should never want disposition for this duty, as we never want matter for it, through the whole course of our lives. Always, even in trials and afflictions, and for all things; being satisfied of their loving intent, and good tendency. God keeps believers from sinning against him, and engages them to submit one to another in all he has commanded, to promote his glory, and to fulfil their duties to each other.
[Eph.5.22-Eph.5.33]
Verses 22-33
The duty of wives is, submission to their husbands in the Lord, which includes honouring and obeying them, from a principle of love to them. The duty of husbands is to love their wives. The love of Christ to the church is an example, which is sincere, pure, and constant, notwithstanding her failures. Christ gave himself for the church, that he might sanctify it in this world, and glorify it in the next, that he might bestow on all his members a principle of holiness, and deliver them from the guilt, the pollution, and the dominion of sin, by those influences of the Holy Spirit, of which baptismal water was the outward sign. The church and believers will not be without spot or wrinkle till they come to glory. But those only who are sanctified now, shall be glorified hereafter. The words of Adam, mentioned by the apostle, are spoken literally of marriage; but they have also a hidden sense in them, relating to the union between Christ and his church. It was a kind of type, as having resemblance. There will be failures and defects on both sides, in the present state of human nature, yet this does not alter the relation. All the duties of marriage are included in unity and love. And while we adore and rejoice in the condescending love of Christ, let husbands and wives learn hence their duties to each other. Thus the worst evils would be prevented, and many painful effects would be avoided.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe duties of children and parents.1–4Of servants and masters.5–9All Christians are to put on spiritual armour against the enemies of their souls.10–18The apostle desires their prayers, and ends with his apostolic blessing.19–24
Children and parents honor God within the family (verses 1–4)

Children have a duty to obey their parents.

True obedience involves inward respect as well as outward compliance.

Throughout history, people who have honored their parents have often experienced the benefits of that discipline.

Parents also have serious duties.

They must avoid impatience and unreasonable harshness.

They should act prudently, explain what is right and seek to convince their children's judgment instead of relying solely on force.

Children should be taught through appropriate, compassionate correction and instruction in the duties God commands.

These responsibilities are often neglected, even in families that profess Christianity.

Some parents' behavior turns their children against religion.

That does not excuse the children's disobedience, but it may have contributed dreadfully to it.

Only God can change a heart.

Yet he often blesses parents' faithful teaching, godly example and prayers.

Parents who care mainly that their children will become wealthy or socially accomplished, while showing little concern for their souls, should not expect God's blessing upon that priority.

Servants and masters are accountable to Christ (verses 5–9)

Paul's teaching addresses the obligations of servants and masters.

Henry notes explicitly that in the ancient setting these servants were generally enslaved people.

The apostles instructed both enslaved workers and their masters in their duties so that wrongs might be reduced, until slavery itself was rooted out through Christianity's influence.

Workers are instructed to act with respect, honesty and faithfulness.

They should not merely pretend to obey while planning to disregard their responsibilities.

Nor should they work well only when their supervisor is watching.

The Lord Jesus sees their service, and devotion to him should make them sincere and diligent in every lawful task.

Work done in love rather than resentment can become easier to perform and pleasing to Christ.

Even humble and exhausting service carried out from duty and for God's glory receives his reward.

Those exercising authority also have obligations.

Act toward those under your authority as you would wish to be treated.

Be fair and show sincere concern for their wellbeing.

Do not be tyrannical, harsh or domineering.

You have a Master in heaven, and before Jesus Christ you and the people working under you are fellow servants.

If everyone remembered their duties toward God and the account they must soon give him, relationships within households would become more just and peaceful.

Put on the whole armor of God (verses 10–18)

Our spiritual struggle requires courage and strength from God.

Those wishing to show genuine grace must seek every necessary grace and put on the whole armor of God, which he supplies.

The armor is meant to be worn throughout the battle.

We cannot lay it aside until our struggle is ended and our course completed.

Our battle is not against human enemies alone, nor only against our remaining sinful nature.

We face an enemy who possesses countless ways to deceive unstable souls.

Evil spirits assault us in the things that concern our souls, seeking to destroy God's image within us.

By grace we must resolve not to yield to Satan.

Resist him and he will flee.

But every concession to evil gives him further ground.

If we doubt the justice of our cause, the faithfulness of our Leader or the strength of our armor, we give him an advantage.

Paul drew his picture from a heavily armored soldier facing fierce attack.

There is no armor for the back—nothing for someone who retreats from Christian duty.

Truth and sincerity are the belt that holds the armor in place.

There can be no true religion without genuine sincerity.

Christ's righteousness credited to us is the breastplate protecting us against God's judgment.

Christ's righteousness implanted within us also strengthens the heart against Satan's attacks.

Resolution protects our legs.

The gospel of peace prepares our feet to stand firmly or move forward over difficult ground.

We need a clear knowledge of the gospel to find proper motives for obedience during trials.

Faith is essential in the hour of temptation.

Like a shield, faith receives Christ and the benefits of redemption, relying on the unseen realities of his promise.

Satan's fiery darts include violent temptations and harsh thoughts about God or ourselves.

Faith applies God's word and Christ's grace to extinguish them.

Salvation is our helmet.

The solid hope of victory and eternal life helps keep our thoughts from being corrupted.

For attack, the apostle names one weapon only: the sword of the Spirit, God's word.

It opposes evil desires and blasphemous thoughts rising from within.

It also answers unbelief and false teaching arriving from outside.

Even one biblical passage understood accurately and used rightly can destroy a powerful temptation or objection.

Prayer holds every piece of our armor together.

We have many responsibilities, but we must keep regular times for prayer.

Formal prayer is not always possible while performing other duties.

Nevertheless, brief prayers lifted to God throughout the day are always appropriate.

Our ordinary thoughts should be directed toward holy things.

Prayer should include public, private, secret, shared, solitary, solemn and spontaneous petitions.

It should contain confession, requests for mercy and thanksgiving.

Every prayer must depend on the Holy Spirit's gracious help and instruction.

Continue praying even when answers seem delayed.

And pray not only for yourself, but for all God's people.

Our enemies are powerful and our strength is small.

But our Redeemer is almighty.

Through his strength we can overcome.

Pray for gospel ministers and receive the blessing (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.19-Eph.6.24" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 19–24</reference>)

The gospel was a mystery until God made it known.

Ministers of Christ are entrusted with proclaiming that revelation.

Even the most gifted and respected ministers need the prayers of ordinary believers.

We should pray especially for servants of Christ exposed to severe danger or hardship through their work.

Paul wished his readers peace, love and faith.

Peace includes reconciliation with God, a clear conscience and harmony among believers.

The Spirit gives the graces that produce faith, love and every Christian virtue.

Paul asked for these gifts to increase even in people who had already begun receiving them.

Every blessing comes from God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Divine grace includes God's favor and every spiritual and earthly good that flows from it.

Such grace belongs to those who sincerely love the Lord Jesus Christ.
classic_reading:
[Eph.6.1-Eph.6.4]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
The duties of children and parents. | (1-4) |
Of servants and masters. | (5-9) |
All Christians are to put on spiritual armour against the enemies of their souls. | (10-18) |
The apostle desires their prayers, and ends with his apostolic blessing. | (19-24) |
Verses 1-4
The great duty of children is, to obey their parents. That obedience includes inward reverence, as well as outward acts, and in every age prosperity has attended those distinguished for obedience to parents. The duty of parents. Be not impatient; use no unreasonable severities. Deal prudently and wisely with children; convince their judgements and work upon their reason. Bring them up well; under proper and compassionate correction; and in the knowledge of the duty God requires. Often is this duty neglected, even among professors of the gospel. Many set their children against religion; but this does not excuse the children's disobedience, though it may be awfully occasion it. God alone can change the heart, yet he gives his blessing to the good lessons and examples of parents, and answers their prayers. But those, whose chief anxiety is that their children should be rich and accomplished, whatever becomes of their souls, must not look for the blessing of God.
[Eph.6.5-Eph.6.9]
Verses 5-9
The duty of servants is summed up in one word, obedience. The servants of old were generally slaves. The apostles were to teach servants and masters their duties, in doing which evils would be lessened, till slavery should be rooted out by the influence of Christianity. Servants are to reverence those over them. They are to be sincere; not pretending obedience when they mean to disobey, but serving faithfully. And they must serve their masters not only when their master's eye is upon them; but must be strict in the discharge of their duty, when he is absent and out of the way. Steady regard to the Lord Jesus Christ will make men faithful and sincere in every station, not grudgingly or by constraint, but from a principle of love to the masters and their concerns. This makes service easy to them, pleasing to their masters, and acceptable to the Lord Christ. God will reward even the meanest drudgery done from a sense of duty, and with a view to glorify him. Here is the duty of masters. Act after the same manner. Be just to servants, as you expect they should be to you; show the like good-will and concern for them, and be careful herein to approve yourselves to God. Be not tyrannical and overbearing. You have a Master to obey, and you and they are but fellow-servants in respect to Christ Jesus. If masters and servants would consider their duties to God, and the account they must shortly give to him, they would be more mindful of their duty to each other, and thus families would be more orderly and happy.
[Eph.6.10-Eph.6.18]
Verses 10-18
Spiritual strength and courage are needed for our spiritual warfare and suffering. Those who would prove themselves to have true grace, must aim at all grace; and put on the whole armour of God, which he prepares and bestows. The Christian armour is made to be worn; and there is no putting off our armour till we have done our warfare, and finished our course. The combat is not against human enemies, nor against our own corrupt nature only; we have to do with an enemy who has a thousand ways of beguiling unstable souls. The devils assault us in the things that belong to our souls, and labour to deface the heavenly image in our hearts. We must resolve by God's grace, not to yield to Satan. Resist him, and he will flee. If we give way, he will get ground. If we distrust either our cause, or our Leader, or our armour, we give him advantage. The different parts of the armour of heavy-armed soldiers, who had to sustain the fiercest assaults of the enemy, are here described. There is none for the back; nothing to defend those who turn back in the Christian warfare. Truth, or sincerity, is the girdle. This girds on all the other pieces of our armour, and is first mentioned. There can be no religion without sincerity. The righteousness of Christ, imputed to us, is a breastplate against the arrows of Divine wrath. The righteousness of Christ implanted in us, fortifies the heart against the attacks of Satan. Resolution must be as greaves, or armour to our legs; and to stand their ground or to march forward in rugged paths, the feet must be shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace. Motives to obedience, amidst trials, must be drawn from a clear knowledge of the gospel. Faith is all in all in an hour of temptation. Faith, as relying on unseen objects, receiving Christ and the benefits of redemption, and so deriving grace from him, is like a shield, a defence every way. The devil is the wicked one. Violent temptations, by which the soul is set on fire of hell, are darts Satan shoots at us. Also, hard thoughts of God, and as to ourselves. Faith applying the word of God and the grace of Christ, quenches the darts of temptation. Salvation must be our helmet. A good hope of salvation, a Scriptural expectation of victory, will purify the soul, and keep it from being defiled by Satan. To the Christian armed for defense in battle, the apostle recommends only one weapon of attack; but it is enough, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. It subdues and mortifies evil desires and blasphemous thoughts as they rise within; and answers unbelief and error as they assault from without. A single text, well understood, and rightly applied, at once destroys a temptation or an objection, and subdues the most formidable adversary. Prayer must fasten all the other parts of our Christian armour. There are other duties of religion, and of our stations in the world, but we must keep up times of prayer. Though set and solemn prayer may not be seasonable when other duties are to be done, yet short pious prayers darted out, always are so. We must use holy thoughts in our ordinary course. A vain heart will be vain in prayer. We must pray with all kinds of prayer, public, private, and secret; social and solitary; solemn and sudden: with all the parts of prayer; confession of sin, petition for mercy, and thanksgiving for favours received. And we must do it by the grace of God the Holy Spirit, in dependence on, and according to, his teaching. We must preserve in particular requests, notwithstanding discouragements. We must pray, not for ourselves only, but for all saints. Our enemies are mighty, and we are without strength, but our Redeemer is almighty, and in the power of his mighty we may overcome. Wherefore we must stir up ourselves. Have not we, when God has called, often neglected to answer? Let us think upon these things, and continue our prayers with patience. ( [Eph.6.19-Eph.6.24] Ep 6:19-24)
[Eph.6.19-Eph.6.24]
Verses 19-24
The gospel was a mystery till made known by Divine revelation; and it is the work of Christ's ministers to declare it. The best and most eminent ministers need the prayers of believers. Those particularly should be prayed for, who are exposed to great hardships and perils in their work. Peace be to the brethren, and love with faith. By peace, understand all manner of peace; peace with God, peace of conscience, peace among themselves. And the grace of the Spirit, producing faith and love, and every grace. These he desires for those in whom they were already begun. And all grace and blessings come to the saints from God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Grace, that is, the favour of God; and all good, spiritual and temporal, which is from it, is and shall be with all those who thus love our Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity, and with them only.
